definition.text: An equilibrium of a market with flexible prices and many traders, each too small to move prices, in which every trader gets the best bundle they can afford and supply equals demand; also called Walrasian equilibrium.

facts.text: Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu introduced the concept in 1951, and it serves as economics' benchmark of efficiency.
If Alice values her car at 10 and Bob at 20, any price between 10 and 20 is an equilibrium price at which Bob buys the car.
The Arrow–Debreu model shows such an equilibrium exists in any exchange economy with divisible goods when everyone's preferences are strictly convex.
By the welfare theorems, every competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient, and every efficient allocation can be reached by one.
At this equilibrium the value society puts on a good equals the value of resources used to make it: marginal benefit equals marginal cost.
Efficiency here says nothing about fairness: an allocation where one person has everything can still be efficient.

definition.text: An ascending auction that finds a competitive equilibrium by raising the price of any item more than one buyer wants until each item is wanted by at most one buyer.

facts.text: The auctioneer starts all prices at zero and buyers name their favourite bundle at each round of prices.
Such mechanisms are also called Walrasian tâtonnement or English auctions.

title: Cost curve

definition.text: A graph showing a firm's production costs against the total quantity it produces.

facts.text: Profit-maximizing firms use cost curves to decide how much to produce.
There are total, average, marginal, fixed and variable cost curves, some for the short run and some for the long run.
Fixed cost is a flat line, while average fixed cost falls as output grows because the same cost is spread over more units.
Short-run marginal cost first falls and then rises because of diminishing marginal returns; the long-run curve is shaped by returns to scale.
When marginal cost is below average cost, average cost falls; when above, it rises; where they are equal, average cost is lowest.
In a 1952 survey of 334 companies, 95% of managers reported constant or falling costs rather than the textbook U-shape.

contested_note: Textbooks draw U-shaped cost curves, but surveys of firms suggest most face constant or falling costs.
